items.readable_text:
Content:
We can describe the velocity of a particle moving in the [MATH: xy]-plane using a velocity vector. The velocity vector tells us the magnitude and direction at which the particle moves. We denote the velocity vector of a particle as [MATH: \mathbf u.]

Content:
As an example, consider the particle [MATH: P] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/aa0404f86406cfa8179b75cc2f37891d]

Content:
In this case, the velocity vector is given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{u} = (3\,\mathbf{i} + 2\,\mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{m/s}.]

Content:
We should think of the particle's velocity as being made up of two components:

Content:
- a horizontal component of [MATH: 3 \: \textrm{m/s}] (moving to the right), and
- a vertical component of [MATH: 2 \: \textrm{m/s}] (moving upward).

Content:
In other words, the particle moves [MATH: 3] meters to the right and [MATH: 2] units up every second. Also, since the horizontal and vertical components are constants, we say that the particle moves with constant velocity.

Content:
The magnitude of the velocity vector gives the speed of the particle. Therefore, in our example, the speed of the particle is

Content:
[MATH: |u||=|3i + 2j|; = sqrt(3^{2} + 2^{2}); = sqrt(9 + 4); = sqrt(13)m/s.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
The acceleration of a particle tells us the rate at which its velocity changes over time. We can use vectors to model the acceleration of a particle moving in the [MATH: xy]-plane.

Content:
For example, consider a particle [MATH: P] whose acceleration vector [MATH: \mathbf a] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf a = (3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})\,\textrm{m/s}^2.]

Content:
We should think of this particle's acceleration as being made up of two components:

Content:
- a horizontal component of [MATH: 3 \: \textrm{m/s}^2] (to the right), and
- a vertical component of [MATH: 4 \: \textrm{m/s}^2] (upward).

Content:
In other words,

Content:
- the horizontal component of the velocity increases by [MATH: 3\,\textrm{m/s}] every second, and
- the vertical component of the velocity increases by [MATH: 4\,\textrm{m/s}] every second.

Content:
Also, since both components are constants, we say that this particle moves with constant acceleration.

Content:
If a particle is moving with constant acceleration, the velocity vector [MATH: \mathbf v] at time [MATH: t] can be found using

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t,]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf{u}] is the velocity of the particle when [MATH: t=0] (i.e., the initial velocity).

Content:
For example, suppose that the initial velocity of our particle is given by [MATH: \mathbf{u} = (2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{m/s}.] What is the particle's velocity when [MATH: t=2 \, \textrm{s}?]

Content:
Substituting our data into the formula above, we obtain that the velocity of the particle will be

Content:
[MATH: v|= u + at; = (2i + 3j) + (3i + 4j)(2); = (2i + 3j) + (6i + 8j); = (8i + 11j)m/s.]

sections.normalized_html: The velocity of a particle is [MATH: (\mathbf{i} -4\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{m/s}] when [MATH: t=0\,\textrm{s}.] If the particle moves with a constant acceleration of [MATH: (2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{m/s}^2,] find the velocity of the particle when [MATH: t=5 \, \textrm{s}.]
sections.readable_text: The velocity of a particle is [MATH: (\mathbf{i} -4\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{m/s}] when [MATH: t=0\,\textrm{s}.] If the particle moves with a constant acceleration of [MATH: (2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{m/s}^2,] find the velocity of the particle when [MATH: t=5 \, \textrm{s}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that when a particle moves with constant acceleration, the velocity vector at time [MATH: t] can be found using

[MATH: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t,]

where [MATH: \mathbf{u}] is the initial velocity, and [MATH: \mathbf{a}] is the acceleration of the particle.

Here, we have

[MATH: \mathbf u = \mathbf{i} -4\mathbf{j}, \qquad \mathbf a = 2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} .]

Therefore, after [MATH: t = 5 \, \textrm{s},] the velocity of the particle will be

[MATH: v|= u + at; = (i − 4j) + (2i + j)(5); = (i − 4j) + (10i + 5j); = (11i + j)m/s.]

Content:

sections.normalized_html: A particle moves with constant acceleration. When [MATH: t=0 \, \textrm{h},] the velocity of the particle is [MATH: 4\mathbf{i} \, \textrm{km/h},] and when [MATH: t=3\, \textrm{h},] the velocity of the particle is [MATH: (7\mathbf{i}+15\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{km/h}.] Calculate the acceleration of the particle.

When [MATH: t=0 \, \textrm{h},] the velocity of the particle is [MATH: 4\mathbf{i} \, \textrm{km/h},] and when [MATH: t=3\, \textrm{h},] the velocity of the particle is [MATH: (7\mathbf{i}+15\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{km/h}.] Calculate the acceleration of the particle.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that when a particle moves with constant acceleration, the velocity vector at time [MATH: t] can be found using

[MATH: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t,]

where [MATH: \mathbf{u}] is the initial velocity, and [MATH: \mathbf{a}] is the acceleration of the particle.

Substituting

[MATH: \mathbf{u} = 4\mathbf{i}, \qquad \mathbf{v} = 7\mathbf{i}+15\mathbf{j}, \qquad t =3]

into the equation above, we can solve for [MATH: \mathbf{a}] as follows:

[MATH: v|= u + at; 7i + 15j|= 4i + a(3); 3i + 15j|= 3a; a|= (1)/(3)(3i + 15j); a|= (i + 5j)km/h^{2}.]

[MATH: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t,]

where [MATH: \mathbf{u}] is the initial velocity, and [MATH: \mathbf{a}] is the acceleration of the particle.

Substituting

[MATH: \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}, \qquad
\mathbf{u} = -\mathbf{i} -\mathbf{j}, \qquad
\mathbf{v} = 3\mathbf{i}+7\mathbf{j}]

into the equation above, we can solve for [MATH: t] as follows:

[MATH: v|= u + at; 3i + 7j|= (− i − j) + (i + 2j)t; 4i + 8j|= (i + 2j)t; 4i + 8j|= ti + 2tj]

Equating the [MATH: \mathbf i] and [MATH: \mathbf j] components in the last equation, we obtain
[MATH: {4 = t; 8 = 2t]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We can describe the velocity of a particle moving in the [MATH: xy]-plane using a velocity vector. The velocity vector tells us the magnitude and direction at which the particle moves. We denote the velocity vector of a particle as [MATH: \mathbf u.]

Content:
As an example, consider the particle [MATH: P] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/aa0404f86406cfa8179b75cc2f37891d]

Content:
In this case, the velocity vector is given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{u} = (3\,\mathbf{i} + 2\,\mathbf{j}) \: \textrm{m/s}.]

Content:
We should think of the particle's velocity as being made up of two components:

Content:
- a horizontal component of [MATH: 3 \: \textrm{m/s}] (moving to the right), and
- a vertical component of [MATH: 2 \: \textrm{m/s}] (moving upward).

Content:
In other words, the particle moves [MATH: 3] meters to the right and [MATH: 2] units up every second. Also, since the horizontal and vertical components are constants, we say that the particle moves with constant velocity.

Content:
The magnitude of the velocity vector gives the speed of the particle. Therefore, in our example, the speed of the particle is

Content:
[MATH: |u||=|3i + 2j|; = sqrt(3^{2} + 2^{2}); = sqrt(9 + 4); = sqrt(13)m/s.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Speed of a Particle Given Its Velocity

Example Prompt:
A particle moves with a constant velocity of [MATH: \mathbf{u}=(5\mathbf{i} +2\mathbf{j}) \,\textrm{km/h}.] Find the speed of the particle.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The speed of a particle equals the magnitude of its velocity.

Therefore, the speed of the particle is

[MATH: |u||=|5i + 2j|; = sqrt(5^{2} + 2^{2}); = sqrt(25 + 4); = sqrt(29)]

kilometers per hour.

Item 5 — Tutorial: Relating Velocity and Acceleration

Content:
The acceleration of a particle tells us the rate at which its velocity changes over time. We can use vectors to model the acceleration of a particle moving in the [MATH: xy]-plane.

Content:
For example, consider a particle [MATH: P] whose acceleration vector [MATH: \mathbf a] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf a = (3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})\,\textrm{m/s}^2.]

Content:
We should think of this particle's acceleration as being made up of two components:

Content:
- a horizontal component of [MATH: 3 \: \textrm{m/s}^2] (to the right), and
- a vertical component of [MATH: 4 \: \textrm{m/s}^2] (upward).

Content:
In other words,

Content:
- the horizontal component of the velocity increases by [MATH: 3\,\textrm{m/s}] every second, and
- the vertical component of the velocity increases by [MATH: 4\,\textrm{m/s}] every second.

Content:
Also, since both components are constants, we say that this particle moves with constant acceleration.

Content:
If a particle is moving with constant acceleration, the velocity vector [MATH: \mathbf v] at time [MATH: t] can be found using

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t,]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf{u}] is the velocity of the particle when [MATH: t=0] (i.e., the initial velocity).

Content:
For example, suppose that the initial velocity of our particle is given by [MATH: \mathbf{u} = (2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{m/s}.] What is the particle's velocity when [MATH: t=2 \, \textrm{s}?]

Content:
Substituting our data into the formula above, we obtain that the velocity of the particle will be

Content:
[MATH: v|= u + at; = (2i + 3j) + (3i + 4j)(2); = (2i + 3j) + (6i + 8j); = (8i + 11j)m/s.]

---

Item 6 — Example: Calculating the Final Velocity of a Particle

Example Prompt:
The velocity of a particle is [MATH: (\mathbf{i} -4\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{m/s}] when [MATH: t=0\,\textrm{s}.] If the particle moves with a constant acceleration of [MATH: (2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{m/s}^2,] find the velocity of the particle when [MATH: t=5 \, \textrm{s}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that when a particle moves with constant acceleration, the velocity vector at time [MATH: t] can be found using

[MATH: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t,]

where [MATH: \mathbf{u}] is the initial velocity, and [MATH: \mathbf{a}] is the acceleration of the particle.

Here, we have

[MATH: \mathbf u = \mathbf{i} -4\mathbf{j}, \qquad \mathbf a = 2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} .]

Therefore, after [MATH: t = 5 \, \textrm{s},] the velocity of the particle will be

[MATH: v|= u + at; = (i − 4j) + (2i + j)(5); = (i − 4j) + (10i + 5j); = (11i + j)m/s.]

---

Item 9 — Example: Calculating the Acceleration of a Particle

Example Prompt:
A particle moves with constant acceleration. When [MATH: t=0 \, \textrm{h},] the velocity of the particle is [MATH: 4\mathbf{i} \, \textrm{km/h},] and when [MATH: t=3\, \textrm{h},] the velocity of the particle is [MATH: (7\mathbf{i}+15\mathbf{j}) \, \textrm{km/h}.] Calculate the acceleration of the particle.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that when a particle moves with constant acceleration, the velocity vector at time [MATH: t] can be found using

[MATH: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t,]

where [MATH: \mathbf{u}] is the initial velocity, and [MATH: \mathbf{a}] is the acceleration of the particle.

Substituting

[MATH: \mathbf{u} = 4\mathbf{i}, \qquad
\mathbf{v} = 7\mathbf{i}+15\mathbf{j}, \qquad
t =3]

into the equation above, we can solve for [MATH: \mathbf{a}] as follows:

[MATH: v|= u + at; 7i + 15j|= 4i + a(3); 3i + 15j|= 3a; a|= (1)/(3)(3i + 15j); a|= (i + 5j)km/h^{2}.]
